title: Polynomial-time complementation of d-DNNFs
formal:
Is there a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that, given any d-DNNF circuit \(C\), outputs a d-DNNF circuit \(D\) over the same variables such that
\[\forall a:X\to\{0,1\},\qquad f_D(a)=1-f_C(a)?\]
The runtime is measured in the explicit binary input encoding and includes writing the entire output. The output may use different decompositions and share subcircuits arbitrarily, subject to the same d-DNNF conditions. It may omit irrelevant input variables, but may not introduce new variables, quantifiers or negation gates above leaves.

One uniform algorithm and one polynomial bound must work for all input sizes and all promised circuits. This is a construction question, distinct from the nonconstructive polynomial-size closure question.
why: Complementation is a basic operation needed to reuse a compiled Boolean representation for exceptions, exclusions and opposite events. General d-DNNFs support useful counting and reasoning tasks, but it is unknown whether this logical transformation can always preserve their computational advantages with polynomial overhead. Resolving the construction question would clarify which operations can be performed directly on this succinct representation.

sentences: The problem asks for a uniform deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that complements any given d-DNNF circuit.
Its output must remain decomposable and deterministic and agree with the Boolean complement on every assignment.
The time bound includes constructing and writing a complete circuit over the original variables.
A polynomial-size complement may conceivably exist without a known efficient construction, so that separate existence question is not the whole target.
Known lower bounds for structured representations leave this general circuit operation unresolved.

context_blocks.text: The source question explicitly separates efficient complementation from existence of a small complement. Every Boolean complement has some d-DNNF representation; the issue is a polynomial bound, and for the computational version a uniform algorithm achieving one.

The knowledge-compilation map treats negation as a transformation with an output representation, separately from queries such as counting satisfying assignments or comparing functions. Its d-DNNF negation entry is unresolved.

Vinall-Smeeth proves a superpolynomial complement-size lower bound when the output must remain structured, even without output determinism. The source leaves unstructured d-DNNF complementation open: removing the global variable-tree restriction changes the target of the lower bound.

The 2026 probabilistic-word paper connects complement gates in tractable circuit representations to the unresolved succinctness question for d-DNNFs. This is evidence of an additional counting-language connection, not a general complement construction or lower bound.

problem_relations.reason: The separate polynomial-size existence question is TCS-7260. A polynomial-time complementation algorithm as asked for here implies a polynomial size bound, but the converse is not established. The two targets are retained separately so that an existence result is not mistaken for an efficient construction.

source_consolidations.note: The knowledge-compilation map asks for polynomial-time negation of deterministic DNNF and its smooth variant. This is constructive closure, including polynomial output size, and is stronger than nonconstructive polynomial-size closure; the latter remains separately represented by TCS-7260.

definitions:
A negation-normal-form Boolean circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with a designated output gate. A leaf is a constant \(0\) or \(1\), or a literal \(x\) or \(\neg x\) for a variable in a finite set \(X\). Each internal gate is AND or OR with a finite nonempty input list. Arbitrary fan-in and sharing of subcircuits are allowed, and every input occurrence counts as an edge. Evaluation on an assignment \(a:X\to\{0,1\}\) uses the ordinary Boolean operations. There are no other negation gates. Constants suffice when \(X\) is empty.

For a gate \(g\), let \(\operatorname{var}(g)\) be the variables appearing in the literals reachable by following its input edges. Decomposability requires that the input subcircuits of each AND gate have pairwise disjoint such variable sets. Determinism requires that, for every OR gate, no assignment to \(X\) makes two distinct input occurrences true simultaneously. A d-DNNF satisfies both conditions at every gate. Determinism is a semantic mutual-exclusion property; it is not a restriction to gates that branch on a single variable.

Write \(f_C(a)\) for the output of circuit \(C\) and \(s(C)=|V(C)|+|E(C)|\) for its size, including leaves and all wires. Unused variables in \(X\) do not affect evaluation. Smoothness, which would require all inputs of an OR gate to mention the same variables, is not assumed. There is also no common tree organizing the variable splits of all conjunction gates. Thus the target uses general d-DNNFs, not only the smaller class of structured d-DNNFs. When two circuits are compared, their variable names denote the same coordinates of a common assignment; a missing coordinate is simply ignored by that circuit.

For computational tasks, encode a circuit as a topologically ordered list of gate records, with gate kinds, signed variable indices at literal leaves, input-list lengths and binary indices of earlier input gates. Include the output index. Variables occurring in the input circuit, or jointly in the two input circuits for a comparison, are consistently renamed to \(1,\ldots,n\); the number \(n\) is at most the total number of input literal occurrences. The input length \(b\) is the total number of bits of these records and delimiters. Gate-and-wire size and bit length are polynomially related with this convention.

An algorithm is one deterministic multitape Turing machine with no oracle, advice or randomness. Polynomial time means at most \(K(b+1)^d\) bit steps for fixed constants \(K,d\) independent of the circuits and number of variables. The inputs are promised to be d-DNNFs. The machine must satisfy the time bound on every input encoding, but its output may be arbitrary when the promise fails; it is not required to recognize the semantic determinism promise. All input reading and output writing count toward the bound.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the existence of such a uniform polynomial-time complementing algorithm. A positive answer must prove the output d-DNNF properties, equality to the complement on every assignment and the full bit-time bound. A negative answer must exclude all deterministic polynomial-time algorithms meeting this promise specification, not merely one construction or one output structure. A polynomial-size existence theorem without an efficient construction does not prove the claim. A conditional lower bound establishes only its stated conditional implication unless the needed assumption is also proved.
